name: Kotter's 8-Step Change Model
use_case: For leaders whose organisation-wide change, such as a new system, a restructuring or a new way of working, keeps losing momentum: the top approves it, staff agree in principle, and a year later little is different because the old habits quietly returned. It sequences the leadership work across the whole programme, from making the need felt and assembling a group with the weight to drive it, through a vision people can repeat and early visible results, to keeping going until the new way is simply how the organisation works.
strengths: gives leaders a shared vocabulary for where a large change programme is weak
names the failure modes that sink most transformations, such as declaring victory too early
insists on visible early results, which keeps sceptics and funders on board
treats the final step, making the change part of everyday practice, as real work rather than an afterthought
widely known, so boards and sponsors accept it without a long explanation
weaknesses: leader-driven by design; the people affected appear mainly as an audience to persuade
drawn as a linear sequence, while real programmes run several steps at once and loop back
evidence comes largely from the author's consulting experience; the whole sequence has not been tested empirically
manufactured urgency can read as alarmism and harden resistance instead
a planning frame, not a diagnostic: it says what leaders should do, not why a particular group is resisting
use_cases: A city administration is moving every department onto one digital case-management system; two earlier rollouts started with fanfare and then faded as offices went back to paper files.

A school district wants all its schools to adopt a new approach to teaching and assessment over several years, and needs principals and teachers still committed long after the first-year enthusiasm has worn off.

After a merger the board announced a new operating model, but middle managers keep running their units the old way and the executive team has no plan for carrying the change through the whole organisation.
A hospital group's executive team has to lead a multi-year transformation of how its departments work together, and previous initiatives were declared a success too early and then unravelled.
A university leadership wants every faculty to move to a new blended-teaching model and must win over sceptical deans and build a broad base of support before the change is announced campus-wide.
